newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iran reaction to verdict "understandable" - Kinkel.
newsitem.headline: Iran reaction to verdict "understandable" - Kinkel.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Sunday it was "more than" understandable a Berlin court verdict concluding Iran's leaders had ordered killings prompted a hefty emotional response in Iran.

In conciliatory remarks, he also said Bonn was taking seriously threats by a radical Islamic group in Iran to unleash suicide attacks against Germany, but assured Germans that Tehran could be taken at its word that they would come to no harm.
"A pause for thought" was needed, he said, urging calm to consider how Germany and the rest of Europe should redefine their battered relations with Tehran.
But he said Iran's political leaders would have to give up their support for terrorism and agree to observe international law before a fresh start could be made.
"The huge emotional reaction to this verdict is more than understandable. I am also outraged. But we must keep calm and realise," he told Hesse Radio in an interview.
"This important country and the Iranian people do not deserve to have relations cut off completely," Kinkel said.
Kinkel's comments came two days after the leader of hardline Ansar-e Hizbollah said his followers were ready to die as martyrs against Germany if ordered by Iran's supreme leader.
They were the latest in a series of conciliatory remarks which won Kinkel praise in the official Tehran Times newspaper on Sunday for insisting Europe must maintain ties with Iran.

The Berlin verdict nearly two weeks ago not only prompted an official protest from Iran's leadership but also unleashed a wave of protests in Tehran where thousands of people took to the streets and some tried to storm the German embassy.

The court said Iranian leaders, including the state president and the religious leader, had ordered the killings. But it only mentioned Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan by name. Iran has repeatedly denied all involvement.

Iranian officials have said they are committed to protecting foreign residents and Kinkel issued a ministry statement on Saturday saying he had no reason to doubt Tehran's assurances the 530 Germans in Iran were safe.
"Of course we are taking the latest threats by the extremist Ansar-e Hizbollah to unleash suicide commandos seriously," the statement quoted Kinkel as saying.

"At the same time, no one in Germany has anything to fear since these suicide commandos apparently only act on orders from the (Iranian) government," he said. Kinkel said he would discuss with his EU counterparts at a meeting of foreign ministers on April 29 the future shape of relations with Iran.

The Berlin court verdict nearly two weeks ago that jailed an Iranian and three Lebanese for the murder of four Kurdish dissidents and accused Tehran of ordering the killings prompted the bloc to abandon its "critical dialogue" policy with Iran.
The policy had been aimed at keeping communications lines with Iran open while trying promote pro-western elements and human rights. Kinkel was widely seen as its chief proponent.
Kinkel's opponents in parliament from the Social Democrats and Greens branded the policy "a complete failure" on Thursday and Greens leader Joschka Fischer called on him to resign.

The verdict was the first time a European court had clearly attributed political responsibility for any of the dozens of assassinations of Iranian opposition figures abroad since the Islamic revolution in Iran in 1979.
